turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Pretorius. Come through, I just need your blood pressure before the doctor calls you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, ja, let's get it over with. It's nothing, hey. I'm only here for the script.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Sit still for me. That's one forty-six over eighty-eight, and your pulse is seventy-six.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's a bit higher than last time, isn't it, Alan?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, it's fine. I rushed from the car, that's all.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Repeat scripts. Knee still the main thing?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just a niggle. Hardly worth talking about. But the pharmacy keeps giving me the weak stuff and I want something that actually works.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Which tablets are you on now?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two of the five hundred ones, three times a day. And the little blood pressure tablet.
[SEG0010] person_1 (NURSE): The pharmacy list says paracetamol five hundred milligrams three times a day, and amlodipine five milligrams once daily.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's wrong. I take two. Wait, two of the five hundreds, so a thousand milligrams, not five hundred. Three times a day. Been doing that for months.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does, Doctor. Two at breakfast, two at lunch, two at supper. I've watched him.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the list and what you take don't match. We'll leave that dose unclear. The amlodipine, every morning?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He misses it. Especially over the weekend when we're with the grandchildren.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any other tablets? Anything stopped?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I used to take Brufen, four hundred milligrams, when the knee was playing up. Stopped it. Made my stomach sour.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did you stop the ibuprofen?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, a couple of months back. Well, actually, I can't give you a date.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Alan, the penicillin. You got that rash when you were younger, and you've avoided it ever since.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): That was years ago, man. I don't count it. I'm not allergic to anything now.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Noted as not agreed. Any swelling in the knee?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pain go down the leg?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Not properly.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Waking at night with it?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I sleep fine.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stiffness in the morning?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): A few minutes, then it goes. Nothing.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not nothing. He holds the wall getting out of bed.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has the knee been like this?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Five years, easy. Maybe more. I don't know, long time.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. It started the season the Proteas toured Australia. That's two years.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between two and five years. I won't pin it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, whatever. Can I get the strong ones? Tramadol, or that Myprodol from the chemist.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. I'm not prescribing tramadol or a codeine mix. Not for this.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Shame, man. The knee is sore when I walk to the shop, that's all I'm saying. Stairs are worse.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Rest eases it?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, if I sit down. And the heat helps a bit, the hot water bottle.
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him about the nights, Alan. Go on.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I do wake. Around two, when I turn over, the knee grabs, and then I'm awake a while. I said I sleep fine, but that's not true.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, so the night waking is there. Any locking, or giving way?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No giving way. Doesn't lock.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Shortness of breath?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Quick look. Knee's not warm, no redness, and I can't feel a big effusion. It bends to about ninety degrees.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): See. Nothing much.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): It still sounds like osteoarthritis in that right knee. Nothing acute on top. Working impression only.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's had the high blood pressure for years as well. You know that.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. Hypertension, ongoing. That's what the amlodipine is for. I'm renewing the existing script, not adding an opioid.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): So no stronger painkiller. Ag, fine.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stay off the ibuprofen. Use the hot water bottle, and don't push the stairs if the knee's grabbing.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): We might do an x-ray of the knee if it has not settled in six weeks.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want a whole lot of tests, hey.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's only if it hasn't settled. Come back in six weeks either way for the script check.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): If I must.
[SEG0059] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if it suddenly gets much worse before then?
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): If it gets worse, or it locks, come back sooner. Don't wait the six weeks.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, fine.
[SEG0062] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print a note for the pharmacy about the dose mismatch so they can query it.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Anything else medical?
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Medically, no. The drive was a nightmare, hey. The robot on William Nicol was out, traffic backed right up.
[SEG0065] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Then the rain came down and we sat there forty minutes. I was going on about that Proteas batting collapse.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, and Thabo, shame, the little one, he hit a six in the garden and smashed the pot plant. Nearly got the dog as well.
[SEG0067] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's only six. Proud as punch. We'll tell you the rest another day or we'll lose the parking.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Six weeks, and sooner if it worsens. Nurse will sort the script at the desk.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp. Cheers, doc.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

omissions.text: Paracetamol dose as actually taken was stated as two 500 mg tablets (1000 mg) three times a day, confirmed by family member; the recorded medication entry omits the dose and tablet count.
Knee pain is in the right knee.
Possible intermittent knee swelling was elicited: patient said 'Sometimes, not really,' indicating swelling is equivocal rather than absent or not asked.
Possible pain radiation down the leg was elicited: patient replied 'Mm, I suppose. Not properly,' indicating equivocal radiation rather than a clear no.

Initial denial of night waking due to knee pain was later corrected by the patient: he wakes around 2 a.m. when turning over and the knee 'grabs,' then stays awake a while. The contradiction itself is clinically relevant.
Doctor documented the penicillin history as 'not agreed' after the patient denied allergy and family member reported a childhood rash; this clinician stance is not captured.
Ibuprofen/Brufen was stopped because it caused stomach upset ('made my stomach sour').
Follow-up in six weeks was specifically for a script check.
